title: reading-notes-llm-serving-oliver-kumar
content:
Top-level intent: quick reading notes and experiment ideas from recent papers/blogs about attention optimizations, kv-cache/serving strategies, and quantization. Purpose is personal: capture key ideas, implications for Redwood Inference runtime, and concrete experiments to try.

1) FlashAttention / memory-efficient attention (paper + blog summary)
- Summary: Reformulate attention computation to avoid explicit large intermediate matrices (softmax on scaled QK^T) and perform fused CUDA kernels to reduce memory bandwidth and peak memory. O(seq^2) compute but much lower memory and faster for long sequences.
- Key takeaways:
  - Significant speedups for long contexts (esp. seq > 2k).
  - Reduces peak memory - enables larger batch/longer context on same GPU.
  - Implementation complexity: need kernel fusion and careful numerics (stable softmax).
- Redwood implications / ideas:
  - For Dedicated and Private deployments, provide a kernel-optimized path that toggles FlashAttention-like implementation at runtime based on sequence length distribution.
  - Add a perf-probe at model load to pick kernel strategy (normal vs fused) given typical batch/seq distribution in a route.
- Experiments to run:
  - Benchmark throughput & memory for 1k/2k/4k contexts on A100 and H100 with and without fused kernels.
  - Measure end-to-end latency variance for tail requests when switching kernel strategy mid-rollout.
- Unresolved questions:
  - How does fused kernel behave with kv-cache streaming (incremental generation)? Need to ensure kv incremental path still benefits.

2) KV-cache sharding and cross-GPU serving paper/blog notes
- Summary: Techniques for sharding KV cache across GPUs to support long-context generation without blowing memory; options include model parallel KV sharding, pipelined token generation (one GPU computes next token while others prepare), or hybrid local prefix caching.
- Key tradeoffs:
  - Sharding reduces per-GPU memory but increases cross-GPU comm and can add latency for each token.
  - Local prefix cache + remote cold storage: frequently accessed prefixes kept local; rare prefixes fetched over network (cache miss).
- Redwood implications:
  - Offer policy-driven KV strategies: local-only (low-latency, high-memory), sharded (memory-efficient), hybrid (cost/latency tradeoff). Surface as route config in Redwood Console.
  - Need telemetry: per-token cross-GPU bytes, RPC latencies, and cache hit rates to drive autoscaling and fallback decisions.
- Experiments to run:
  - Simulate workloads with long-chat sessions (avg context 8k, 50k tokens lifetime) and evaluate cost + latency for local vs sharded KV.
  - Build microbench: single-token p99 latency while varying interconnect bandwidth to see breakpoints.

3) Int4 / Mixed-precision quantization practical notes (blog + repo experiments)
- Summary: Recent practical recipes (GPTQ, data-free calibrations) allow int4 quantization with acceptable quality for many workloads, but per-layer sensitivity varies. Some layers require per-channel scales and outlier handling.
- Key points:
  - Post-training quantization + small calibration set can be surprisingly good for chat assistants, but eval-sensitive tasks (code, math) may regress.
  - Per-head or per-outlier treatment helps; simple static quantization sometimes fails for emergent behaviors.
- Redwood implications:
  - Provide quantization profiles per model in model catalog: e.g., FP16 (default), int8 fast, int4 low-cost (with quality guardrails).
  - Implement automated eval harness: run a small representative eval set per-profile to detect regressions before making profile available as a rollout option.
- Experiments to run:
  - Take 3 open models (LLaMA2 family): generate on standard evals (HHH, GSM8K, HumanEval) for FP16, int8, int4 with GPTQ. Compare logits divergence and qualitative errors.
  - Track cost delta (tokens/sec, GPU memory) vs quality.

4) Systems/ops notes: rollout, routing, and fallback
- Observations: Many production incidents are from unexpected distribution shifts (longer prompts, system prompt injection, heavy embedding workloads). We need automated safeguards.
- Quick ideas:
  - Route-by-policy: prefer cheaper quantized model if latency SLO allows, fallback to FP16 on quality regression or high perplexity.
  - Canary evals running on live traffic shadow copies to detect silent regressions (drop in BLEU/LM-scores on sampled prompts).
  - Add "cost budget" alerting: per-customer token cost trending > threshold triggers a review and optional automatic throttle.

5) Personal to-dos (short, actionable)
- Short-term (this sprint):
  - Spin up benchmark harness: seq lengths 512/1k/2k/4k on A100 and H100; test FlashAttention kernel vs baseline. (Owner: me)
  - Prototype a simple KV sharding microservice (single-node with two processes to mimic cross-GPU) and measure per-token overhead. (Owner: me + Aisha)
- Medium-term:
  - Build quantization eval pipeline integrated with model catalog so profiles have metric cards. (Owner: eng-applied-ml)
  - Design a Console UI for "inference profile" selection per route with warnings/estimated unit cost. (Owner: product/console-and-rollouts)

6) Quick links & refs (copy for later)
- FlashAttention paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09084
- GPTQ repo / quantization notes: https://github.com/IST-DASLab/gptq
- KV sharding / serving notes (internal draft): CON-1423

7) Notes-to-self / loose thoughts (messy)
- Consider adding a perf probe at route creation that runs a tiny synthetic benchmark to pick default kernel/quantization for that route. This could reduce surprise regressions.
- Explore hybrid storage: LRU local prefix cache + remote append-only cold store (s3-like) for very long histories; eviction policy needs to consider generation locality.
- Remember to check how existing batching logic interacts with fused kernels: batching heuristics may need to be more aware of sequence-length skew.
- Write up short doc for Solutions Eng: "When to pick quantized vs FP16" for customer conversations.

End of notes. Save as draft and iterate after experiments.
